author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the structural components of DNA and describe their assembly into a double helix.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A-T, G-C) and explain the hydrogen bonding basis for these pairings.
Describe the antiparallel orientation of DNA strands and relate it to 5'-to-3' backbone directionality.
Trace the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.
Explain the mechanistic basis for continuous leading-strand and discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis.
Articulate why DNA replication is semiconservative and predict daughter molecule composition after successive rounds of replication.

modules.moduleName: The Double Helix: Structure of DNA
modules.description: An interactive exploration of the 3D structure of DNA, including the sugar-phosphate backbones, nitrogenous bases, base pairing, and antiparallel strand orientation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the sugar-phosphate backbone, nitrogenous bases, and hydrogen bonds as structural components of DNA.
Apply complementary base-pairing rules (A-T, G-C) and explain the difference in hydrogen bond number between pairs.
Describe the antiparallel orientation of the two DNA strands and its relationship to 5'-to-3' directionality.
instructions: Observe the double helix model as it rotates and highlights different components.
Pay attention to how base pairs form across the helix axis.
Note the direction labels on each backbone strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the helix model already rotating; slows rotation slightly and displays the title label so students orient themselves to the overall structure before components are highlighted.
clips.narration: Welcome. Here we see the DNA double helix — two strands of sugar-phosphate backbone spiraling around a shared axis. Let's slow down the rotation to examine it closely.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the two backbone strands by enlarging them slightly and brightening their colors, drawing attention to their separate identities before base pairing is introduced.
clips.narration: Each strand consists of a sugar-phosphate backbone. Notice the blue backbone on one side and the orange backbone on the other — these run in opposite directions, which we'll return to shortly.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveals and enlarges the two base pair objects to emphasize the complementary base-pairing rule and the different hydrogen bond counts between A-T and G-C pairs.
clips.narration: Projecting inward from each backbone are the four nitrogenous bases: adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine. Adenine always pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, shown in green. Guanine always pairs with cytosine via three hydrogen bonds, shown in purple — one extra bond makes G-C pairs more stable.

clips.changeMeaning: Adds directional 5' and 3' text labels to each backbone strand to visually anchor the antiparallel concept, and updates the title label to reflect this new focus.
clips.narration: Notice that one backbone runs 5' to 3' from top to bottom, while its partner runs 3' to 5' — this antiparallel arrangement is essential to how the strands fit together and, as we'll see, how replication proceeds.

modules.moduleName: DNA Replication at the Replication Fork
modules.description: A guided walkthrough of semiconservative DNA replication, showing helicase unwinding, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase synthesis, and the asymmetric formation of leading and lagging strands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork.
Explain why the leading strand is synthesized continuously while the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments.
Articulate why replication is semiconservative and predict daughter strand composition after one and two rounds of replication.
instructions: Watch as helicase unwinds the parental double helix.
Observe how single-strand binding proteins stabilize the exposed strands.
Track the movement of DNA polymerase on the leading and lagging strands.
Note how Okazaki fragments are joined by DNA ligase.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the helicase enzyme at the fork and begins visually separating the parental helix into two strands to represent unwinding.
clips.narration: Replication begins when the enzyme helicase binds to the double helix and unwinds it, breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs and creating a replication fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveals single-strand binding proteins along the separated strands to show their stabilizing role immediately after unwinding.
clips.narration: As the strands separate, single-strand binding proteins coat the exposed single strands, preventing them from re-annealing or forming secondary structures.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the leading-strand polymerase and repositions it closer to the fork to depict continuous synthesis in a single direction.
clips.narration: DNA polymerase can only synthesize new DNA in the 5' to 3' direction. On the leading strand template, this allows continuous synthesis directly following the replication fork.

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the lagging-strand polymerase and introduces visible Okazaki fragments to contrast discontinuous synthesis with the continuous leading strand.
clips.narration: On the other template strand, which runs in the opposite direction, DNA polymerase must synthesize discontinuously, moving away from the fork in short segments called Okazaki fragments.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces DNA ligase near the Okazaki fragments and merges the fragments' color to indicate they have been joined into a continuous strand.
clips.narration: Finally, DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments, joining them into one continuous lagging strand.

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the title label to summarize the semiconservative nature of replication, concluding the module with the key conceptual takeaway.
clips.narration: Because each daughter helix retains one original parental strand paired with one newly synthesized strand, this process is called semiconservative replication. After two rounds, each of the four resulting molecules will contain exactly one strand descended from the original parental DNA.
